title: Normalized membrane ratio of TROP2 as a predictor of clinical outcomes with datopotamab deruxtecan in non-small-cell lung cancer
desc: Datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd)—a trophoblast cell surface antigen 2 (TROP2)-directed antibody–drug conjugate—has demonstrated efficacy in patients with advanced nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ± actionable genomic alterations. However, TROP2 expression by pathologist assessment using conventional immunohistochemistry with visual scoring does not predict response to TROP2-directed antibody–drug conjugates in NSCLC. We developed TROP2 quantitative continuous scoring (QCS)—a fully supervised computational pathology approach that quantifies TROP2 expression in individual NSCLC cells and subcellular components from immunohistochemistry-stained slides. Using QCS to determine TROP2 expression at the tumor cell membrane and cytoplasm, normalized membrane ratio (NMR) was developed (ratio of membrane relative to membrane + cytoplasmic TROP2) in the biomarker-evaluable population of patients with advanced NSCLC in the TROPION-PanTumor01 study (n = 115). The TROP2 NMR cut-point was optimized and validated in patients with nonsquamous NSCLC without actionable genomic alterations (primary intended-use population, n = 221) in the biomarker-evaluable population (n = 352) of the TROPION-Lung01 trial. Association with clinical outcomes was assessed. Progression-free survival was longer in Dato-DXd-treated (median 7.2 versus 4.0 months; hazard ratio 0.40, 95% confidence interval 0.25–0.64) but not docetaxel-treated (median 4.1 versus 4.4 months; hazard ratio 0.94, 95% confidence interval 0.59–1.49) patients with TROP2 NMR-positive versus TROP2 NMR-negative samples (treatment by biomarker status interaction P = 0.0098), indicating that TROP2 NMR may be a predictive biomarker for Dato-DXd.

title: DeepTNR: predicting tumor drug sensitivity from spatial transcriptomics with deep graph contrastive and transfer learning
desc: Heterogeneity within the tumor microenvironment remains a major obstacle to precision oncology. Although existing drug-sensitivity models can capture transcriptional heterogeneity, they generally do not account for the spatial organization of predicted drug responses. Here, we developed DeepTNR, a spatially resolved framework that integrates tumor-stroma interface features, spatial autocorrelation, and distance-dependent associations between local cellular composition and predicted drug sensitivity. Across nine tumor types, with colorectal cancer (CRC) as a representative example, DeepTNR identified irinotecan as the most sensitive drug and revealed significant spatial autocorrelation in its predicted response patterns. Spatial proximity effect analysis further showed that local enrichment of immune and proliferative programs positively was associated with increased irinotecan sensitivity. Together, these findings demonstrate the potential of DeepTNR to resolve intratumoral therapeutic heterogeneity and identify niche-specific vulnerabilities.

title: Speak before the reveal: a practical method to protect clinical reasoning from artificial intelligence scribe deskilling, never-skilling, and mis-skilling.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes are rapidly becoming normalized in clinical practice, yet governance frameworks focus on accuracy, privacy, consent, and medicolegal status. Risks to clinician capabilities have received less attention. Speak before the reveal is a proposed method in which clinicians verbalize critical cognitive steps, such as synthesis and plan, before note generation. Recent work distinguishes deskilling in senior clinicians, never-skilling from premature offload in trainees and mis-skilling, the internalization of AI errors and inappropriate use as sound practice. This Perspective builds on emerging evidence that reasoning before seeing AI output may protect unaided reasoning. Training implementation, evaluation, adherence challenges, validation methodology, and governance strategies for training bodies, health services, and scribe vendors are discussed. Speak before the reveal is a low-cost, testable approach to maintaining clinical reasoning for individuals or organizations. Successful AI scribe adoption requires preserving clinicians' ability to work without AI support.

title: [Articles] Detecting low left ventricular ejection fraction from ECG using an interpretable and scalable predictor-driven framework: a model development and validation study
desc: Diagnostic scores of conventional ECG findings from ECG foundation models contain information relevant to the detection of ventricular dysfunction. These representations can be directly reused for low LVEF detection and further integrated into interpretable predictive models, providing a scalable and extensible computational framework for existing AI-ECG systems. Future research should validate the framework in population-based screening settings and larger international cohorts.

title: The digital health ecosystem in respiratory medicine: from traditional testing to real-world, artificial intelligence-powered monitoring and personalised care.
desc: [Breathe (Sheffield, England)] Lung function evaluation is rapidly evolving beyond laboratory testing. While conventional tests remain the clinical reference standard, digital health technologies now enable respiratory assessment at home and in real-world settings through home-based systems, portable devices, and wearables. These tools can support repeated or continuous monitoring of traditional and digital biomarkers of respiratory health and disease. However, they differ in physiological detail, usability, degree of patient involvement and clinical maturity. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an important complement to these technologies. Machine learning and deep learning can support signal processing, quality control and interpretation of pulmonary function tests, while also extracting clinically relevant information from multimodal respiratory data collected outside controlled environments. Generative AI has a more emerging role, mainly in patient communication and educational support. For pulmonary function test interpretation, current evidence supports clinician-AI collaboration as the most realistic near-term model, rather than fully autonomous decision-making. This review summarises the main technologies currently available for lung function evaluation in adults and discusses the current and future role of AI in respiratory monitoring, interpretation and personalised care.

title: Mixed Signals: Weight-Space Programming for EEG and ECG
desc: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to ``training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using 6times fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.

title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents
desc: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance relies on spontaneous adverse event reporting and labor-intensive observational studies, which suffer from underreporting and delayed risk detection. Large language model (LLM) agents could automate real-world evidence generation, but generalist agents make ad hoc analytical decisions that compromise epidemiological validity and reproducibility. Here we present MedCheckpoint, a multi-agent LLM system for automated postmarketing pharmacovigilance. MedCheckpoint grounds each analytical stage in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base, locks core study-design parameters before execution, performs patient-level analyses with human-written deterministic statistical tools, and enforces checkpoint rules that abort infeasible analyses, with optional human-in-the-loop review. We evaluated MedCheckpoint using a 54-question benchmark on a dual-purpose simulated electronic health record (EHR) testbed of 2.7 million individuals, designed with reliable clinical signals to evaluate routine analytical accuracy alongside spurious signals to stress-test system rigor. Across the benchmark, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in report quality across five dimensions rated by three independent LLM judges (overall means 4.81-4.88 versus 4.25-4.55 and 4.02-4.29) and yielded higher run-to-run consistency (mean within-question standard deviation 0.116-0.186 versus up to 0.440). Crucially, while baselines failed on up to 2 of 21 runs when handling infeasible comparisons or unmeasurable outcomes, MedCheckpoint produced no misleading failures across all seven stress-test trap questions with known data limitations. MedCheckpoint enables reliable, auditable, and scalable pharmacovigilance analysis.

title: Multimodal protein representations across human brain cell types
desc: The central nervous system (CNS) comprises diverse cell types whose molecular context shapes the roles of the proteins they express. Computational models offer a scalable way to study the roles of proteins across human brain cell types, with protein language models and interactome- or single-cell-based models capturing complementary information encoded in protein sequences and cellular network contexts. Human brain tissue is hard to access, so brain cell types make up a small fraction of the atlases single-cell models train on and of the benchmarks used for their evaluation. To capture these complementary sources of information in the CNS, we introduce SEMPER, a multimodal representation learning model that aligns protein language model representations with protein-protein interaction networks from 442 cell types of the adult human brain, giving each protein a sequence-informed representation in every cell type in which its gene is expressed. We show that SEMPER representations predict cell type-specific protein complexes and predict genes essential to the survival of dopaminergic neurons, measured in a genome-wide CRISPR screen. In zero-shot retrieval, SEMPER recovers clinically pursued drug targets for Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, Huntington's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis at higher rates than cell type-specific models. To further improve target recovery, we combine SEMPER with a large language model that reasons over protein functional annotations. The combination recovers more targets, with SEMPER providing experimentally derived cellular context that complements literature-based reasoning of the large language model.

Effect of two common GVHD prophylaxis regimens on the gut microbiome in a randomized phase 3 trial
desc: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation can cure certain hematological disorders but has many complications. In retrospective studies, low gut microbiome diversity is associated with adverse clinical outcomes. In 2023, the Blood and Marrow Transplant Clinical Trials Network 1703 randomized phase 3 trial demonstrated the superiority of post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) and mycophenolate mofetil to tacrolimus and methotrexate (Tac/MTX) for graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis in participants with hematological malignancies undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation. Here we report on the microbiome-focused companion study to 1703, Blood and Marrow Transplant Clinical Trials Network 1801, which coenrolled participants and shared trial registration. The primary endpoint was association between microbiome diversity at neutrophil engraftment and non-relapse mortality after 1 year; secondary endpoints included associations with other clinical outcomes and with baseline microbiome diversity. Based on 2575 longitudinally collected stool samples from 304 participants (Tac/MTX n = 147, PTCy n = 157), no association between engraftment microbiome diversity and non-relapse mortality was observed (P = 0.314), not meeting the primary endpoint. Lower baseline microbiome diversity was associated with shorter overall survival (P = 0.007). Safety data were reported in the original 1703 publication. In exploratory analyses, microbiome diversity and absolute microbial load were lower in PTCy compared to Tac/MTX on days 14–28 following HCT, independent of non-prophylaxis antibiotics exposure. Microbial domination events, when a single species exceeds 30% relative abundance, did not differ significantly between study arms and reflected both pathogen blooms and less severe disruptions of the microbial community. Clostridium scindens and secondary bile-acid metabolism pathways were less prevalent in PTCy than in Tac/MTX following HCT. In summary, we find prophylaxis regimens likely exert independent effects on both the microbiome and immune compartments and can also impact their interaction. Understanding whether and how microbiome-targeted interventions might improve transplant outcomes will therefore require careful disentangling of these effects within each specific treatment context. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03959241.

title: Artificial intelligence in dermatophytosis: Toward better clinical diagnosis and management.
desc: [Journal de mycologie medicale] Dermatophytosis is one of the most common superficial fungal infections worldwide. However, its diagnosis and management remain challenging because its clinical manifestations often overlap with those of other dermatoses, conventional mycological tests have inherent limitations, the disease is prone to recurrence, and antifungal resistance has received increasing attention. This review summarizes current applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in dermatophytosis, with a focus on the use of machine learning and deep learning in clinical photographs, non-invasive skin imaging, and laboratory diagnostics, while also discussing their roles in treatment support, follow-up assessment, patient education, and adherence management. In addition, with the accumulation of molecular diagnostic, mass spectrometric, and epidemiological data, AI may also provide auxiliary support for extended applications such as resistance risk recognition. Current evidence suggests that AI can improve the efficiency, consistency, and objectivity of dermatophytosis diagnosis and provide quantitative support for treatment response assessment and long-term follow-up. With further improvement in research quality and the accumulation of clinical application experience, AI is expected to become increasingly integrated into dermatophytosis management workflows.

title: AToP: An Explainability Framework for Transformer-Based EHR Predictions Using Attribution-Guided Temporal Pattern Mining
desc: Objective: To develop and evaluate AToP (Attribution to Temporal Patterns), a post-hoc explainability framework that converts per-token Integrated Gradients (IG) from a Transformer into structured temporal pattern narratives. Materials and Methods: AToP was applied to a single-stream Transformer trained on MIMIC-IV v3.1 (218,196 patients; 12.6% unplanned 30-day readmission). It mines frequent episodes from salient-token subsequences in the training cohort, aggregates attribution among patients whose records contain each token or pattern, and collapses near-duplicates by patient overlap. Validation used masking, reversed-order analysis, token-level faithfulness tests, and KernelSHAP comparison. Results: The Transformer achieved AUROC 0.77 and PR-AUC 0.34. Population-weighted attribution emphasized high-prevalence codes with small per-patient impact. Carrier-conditional attribution, the mean among patients with the token, surfaced rare high-attribution psychiatric markers including psychosis, self-harm overdose, suicidal ideation (SI), and severe major depressive disorder (MDD). Pattern-level attribution identified within-visit co-occurrences and cross-visit trajectories not captured by token rankings. Risk-increasing patterns included psychiatric sequences ({MDD, SI} [->] SI) and oncologic progressions (cancer anemia [->] ascites). Obstetric and chest pain evaluation patterns were associated with lower predicted readmission. Discussion: The framework provides two complementary views of model predictions: carrier-conditional aggregation highlights rare, highly attributed clinical features, while temporal pattern analysis identifies within-visit combinations and cross-visit trajectories missed by token-level rankings. Masking and visit-order reversal provided evidence of correspondence with model behavior, but pattern attributions do not represent unique effects or establish clinical validity. Conclusion: AToP turns a Transformer's attributions into visit-anchored temporal pattern narratives, showing which events, in which order, contribute to its readmission predictions.

title: Rediscovering neuroblastoma pathology from the perspective of digital pathology and AI: Current challenges and future implications.
desc: [Pathologica] Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid malignancy of childhood and demonstrates marked clinical and biologic heterogeneity. Histopathologic evaluation, particularly through the International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification system, remains central to risk stratification by integrating patient age, degree of neuroblastic differentiation, Schwannian stromal development, and the mitosis-karyorrhexis index. However, diagnostic interpretation is challenged by intratumoral heterogeneity, sampling bias, interobserver variability, and the subjective assessment of subtle morphologic thresholds. These limitations directly influence prognostic categorization and subsequent clinical management. Digital pathology, through whole-slide imaging, provides a platform for standardized visualization and quantitative analysis of entire tumor sections. Recent computational and artificial intelligence-assisted approaches have demonstrated feasibility in tumor category classification, assessment of differentiation, automated mitosis-karyorrhexis index quantification, prognostic stratification, and prediction of molecular features such as MYCN amplification. While reported performance metrics are promising, most studies remain retrospective, single-institution studies, and limited by small pediatric datasets. Significant barriers to clinical translation persist, including the need for multi-institutional validation, workflow standardization, quality assurance frameworks, regulatory governance, and mitigation of algorithmic bias. Current evidence supports the role of digital and artificial intelligence tools as complementary aids rather than replacements for expert pathologist interpretation. Coordinated efforts addressing validation, infrastructure readiness, and ethical considerations will be essential for responsible integration of computational methods into neuroblastoma histopathology.

title: Beyond one-off training: Continuing support, system stability and worker-borne costs shape electronic community health reporting in Kisii County, Kenya
desc: Kenya's electronic community health information system (eCHIS) moves household and service data from community health promoters' phones into the national health information system. When reporting quality falls short, the usual response is more training and competency frameworks. We tested whether user capability and one-off training explain how well the system performs for its users, or whether continuing support and system stability matter more. We also examined where along the reporting chain quality was lost. In this convergent mixed-methods cross-sectional study in Kisii County, we surveyed 343 eCHIS users in 22 facility catchments, observed five sites against a structured checklist, and interviewed 13 key informants. Hierarchical ordinal and logistic regression with facility-clustered standard errors modelled user satisfaction and perceived system consistency. Formal eCHIS training was near universal (94.5%) and was not associated with either outcome. Adding continuing support (refresher training, mentorship and technical support response time) significantly improved both models. McFadden's pseudo-R{superscript 2} for consistency rose from 0.06 to 0.16. Each faster level of technical support response almost doubled the odds of reporting a consistent system (adjusted odds ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.35-2.58). Each step up in crash frequency reduced the odds of higher satisfaction (0.60, 0.43-0.84). Digital comfort remained independently associated with both outcomes. At the observation sites, form logic secured completeness (all required fields were filled at 5 of 5 sites), but timeliness (2 of 5), consistency over time (1 of 5) and use of reports for decisions (0 of 4) failed, mostly because of synchronisation. In open-ended responses, 43.4% of respondents raised the cost of data bundles. Informants described promoters paying for connectivity and reinstalling the failing application themselves. Reporting quality depended less on what users knew than on the support around them. Competency frameworks will need matching standards for connectivity financing, support response and synchronisation monitoring.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Orthopedic Image Analysis: A Systematic Review and Unified Taxonomy of Bone Age Assessment and Fracture Detection.
source: PubMed · Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
desc: [Journal of imaging informatics in medicine] Bone age assessment (BAA) and fracture detection are essential tasks in orthopedic radiography, since they aid diagnosis and clinical decision-making in trauma treatment. Recent technologies in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL), have enhanced the ability to analyze radiological images with greater accuracy and consistency. However, current studies are incomplete, with inconsistent evaluation methodologies, limited external validation, and insufficient interpretability, limiting clinical implementation. This study provides a systematic PRISMA-based review of 116 studies (2017-2025) that analyze imaging modalities, datasets, model architectures, evaluation techniques, and clinical relevance. A uniform taxonomy is introduced to define techniques based on task, modality, and learning paradigm, along with a comparative methodology to address inconsistencies across studies. The findings indicate that CNN and transformer-based models achieve MAE as low as 0.4-0.7 years and accuracy exceeding 95% in controlled datasets but are limited by dataset bias, poor generalization, and a lack of standardized benchmarks. Although explainable AI (XAI) approaches increase interpretability, their clinical reliability is still limited. This review synthesizes current methodologies, identifies key problems, and proposes future directions for AI systems that are robust, interpretable, and clinically deployable, while unifying BAA and fracture detection under a single taxonomy that integrates modality, task, and learning paradigm.

AI-Integrated multimodal neuroimaging in Alzheimer's disease: toward biologically informed precision diagnostics.
source: PubMed · Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
desc: [Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association] Alzheimer's disease (AD), which is characterized by the progressive accumulation of amyloid beta plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), metabolic dysfunction, and neuroinflammation, is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder. The distinct pathological features of AD can be characterized in vivo via neuroimaging: Structural magnetic resonance imaging captures brain atrophy, while positron emission tomography detects Aβ/NFT deposition. The application of artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance the interpretation of neuroimaging data, but single-modality AI provides only limited biological information. This limitation has motivated the development of multimodal approaches that integrate complementary imaging, molecular, and clinical data for diagnosis and prognosis. However, there has been no comprehensive examination of how modality-specific neuroimaging information is incorporated into single-modality AI and subsequently integrated within multimodal frameworks. This review addresses this gap by evaluating conventional neuroimaging, single-modality AI, and multimodal AI as part of a unified framework, with particular emphasis on the added diagnostic and prognostic value of multimodal integration. We further identify key methodological and translational bottlenecks in developing clinically robust multimodal AI, including cross-modal and cross-cohort heterogeneity, model complexity, missing modalities, interpretability, and generalizability. Finally, we propose a translational roadmap emphasizing data harmonization, independent external validation, clinically meaningful explainability, and prospective evaluation. Ultimately, the clinical value of multimodal AI will depend on whether its added predictive value is reproducible across independent populations and translates into meaningful improvements in clinical decision-making and patient outcomes.

Towards end-to-end LLM-based censoring-aware survival analysis.
desc: [Journal of biomedical informatics] Survival analysis is central to medical prediction, yet large language models (LLMs) are rarely used as end-to-end survival models because censoring prevents straightforward supervised fine-tuning. Here we present LLMSurvival, a framework that enables censoring-aware survival analysis with unmodified LLMs operating directly on tabular clinical data. LLMSurvival reformulates time-to-event prediction as pairwise ranking among comparable subjects, and derives test-time risk by aggregating comparisons against anchor individuals from the training cohort. Across two clinical tasks (ICU mortality prediction in MIMIC-IV and fragility fracture prediction in a NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medicine cohort), LLMSurvival improves overall concordance over Cox proportional hazards modeling by 3.1% for ICU mortality and 0.5% for fracture risk, and by 2.1% on average for ICU mortality and 2.8% for fracture risk over three established deep learning survival models. The results show that survival modeling with censoring can be made compatible with LLM fine-tuning through comparison-based reformulation. The framework demonstrates high portability and superior performance over expert-curated scores like SAPS-II and FRAX scores across diverse clinical contexts. Furthermore, the framework supports local deployment, as compact, publicly available base models provide sufficient performance. The LLMSurvival framework serves as a proof of concept for an integrated, censoring-conscious approach to survival analysis via LLMs.

Biophotonics in oral health: bridging light-based innovation and clinical practice.
desc: [Frontiers in oral health] Biophotonics is reshaping oral healthcare by transitioning light-based technologies from isolated procedural applications toward integrated diagnostic, therapeutic, and regenerative strategies. Among these approaches, photobiomodulation (PBM) therapy has achieved substantial clinical visibility due to its capacity to modulate inflammation, pain, mitochondrial metabolism, vascular responses, and tissue repair without producing destructive thermal effects. While oral and oropharyngeal mucositis represent the most clinically and quantitatively mature models for PBM, its applications now encompass salivary dysfunction, periodontal therapy, oral surgery, temporomandibular disorders (TMD), implant osseointegration, orthodontics, and inflammatory mucosal conditions. However, translating positive biological outcomes into routine practice remains limited by substantial heterogeneity in device architectures, wavelengths, beam profiles, and reporting standards. This comprehensive narrative review examines the physical, clinical, and dosimetric landscape of oral biophotonics. We address critical gaps in current literature-including reporting shortfalls, negative clinical trials, and general safety risks-and outline the technological evolution toward target-tissue dosimetry. By integrating computational photon-transport models, biological monitoring, and artificial intelligence-assisted dosimetry, we propose a transitional framework toward precision oral photomedicine, wherein anatomical and optical tissue properties guide individualized, patient-centered light delivery.

title: Minnies winners for 2026, Page 2
[Generative artificial intelligence in orthopedics and trauma surgery-Guidelines for responsible use in undergraduate and continuing education].
source: PubMed · Zeitschrift fur Orthopadie und Unfallchirurgie
desc: [Zeitschrift fur Orthopadie und Unfallchirurgie] Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become an established part of medical education and postgraduate training. Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT are widely used for information retrieval, structuring complex content, and preparing clinical cases-often in an informal manner, without didactic guidance and without a clear understanding of how these systems function. For orthopedics and trauma surgery (O&T), a specialty characterized by high decision density and direct responsibility for patient safety, the key question is therefore no longer whether generative AI is used, but how it should be integrated. This article analyzes current patterns of use and highlights a central discrepancy: widespread adoption contrasts with heterogeneous levels of competence. Generative AI can support the structuring of learning processes, simulate elements of clinical reasoning, and assist educators in developing teaching materials. At the same time, LLMs generate responses on a probability-based foundation and do not perform their own evidence verification. Plausible but incorrect information, loss of clinical context, or bias may influence diagnostic reasoning and undermine evidence-based decision-making. In a safety-critical field such as O&T, this necessitates clear orientation and professional standards. The core of the article is the development of a discipline-specific framework for the integration of generative AI into undergraduate and postgraduate education. This framework combines an understanding of how generative AI systems operate with didactic responsibility, quality assurance, and a clear delineation of medical decision-making authority. Generative AI is positioned consistently as a supportive tool, not as a substitute for clinical expertise. Particular emphasis is placed on structured prompting as a key competence. The ability to formulate precise clinical questions, make contextual information explicit, and critically compare AI-generated outputs with guidelines and scientific literature is described as an integral component of contemporary medical professionalism. In addition, the article proposes a practice-oriented guideline for students, residents, and educators. Its aim is to transform the currently informal use of generative AI into a quality-assured, competence-based integration within existing curricula. Educators, trainers, and professional societies are identified as central actors who must shape responsible AI use through clear s

title: Large language model-enhanced decision tree framework for identifying multiple sclerosis diagnoses from clinical documentation.
source: PubMed · Multiple sclerosis and related disorders
desc: [Multiple sclerosis and related disorders] Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial in multiple sclerosis (MS), yet diagnostic delays are common. Large language models (LLMs) such as generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs) may streamline diagnostic workflows by extracting MS diagnostic signals from clinical notes. To derive MS diagnosis status from the first neurology note using a computable algorithm based on the 2017 McDonald criteria and applying GPT-4 for node-level reasoning within a structured decision framework. We analyzed the first neurology notes from 125 randomly selected patients (people with MS, related disorders, and controls) enrolled in a clinic-based cohort between 2017 and 2023. We included the clinical history and diagnostic testing sections but redacted the assessment and plan. We converted the 2017 McDonald criteria into a decision tree and provided expert-curated clinical knowledge to guide GPT-4 reasoning at each decision node. GPT-4 generated binary decisions at each node to traverse the tree and assign MS diagnoses at terminal nodes. We evaluated performance against neurologist-assessed diagnoses and characterized hallucination types (non-factual, incongruent, irrelevant, over-reliant, and logical reasoning errors). In this study cohort (mean age 40±12 years; 81% women) representative of the clinic population, GPT-4 performed well in predicting MS diagnosis (84% accuracy, 79% precision, 74% recall, 91% specificity) using first neurology notes. Hallucinations occurred in 32 cases (26%), most commonly incoherence (75%) and overreliance (47%). A structured, LLM-guided decision framework can identify MS diagnoses from early clinical documentation. Large-scale studies are needed to mitigate hallucinations, validate this approach, and test implementation in clinical settings.

title: From laboratory metrics to clinical value: linking performance to clinical outcomes.
source: PubMed · Scandinavian journal of clinical and laboratory investigation
desc: [Scandinavian journal of clinical and laboratory investigation] Laboratory performance is commonly assessed using indicators such as turnaround time, analytical quality, workload, and operating costs. These measures are useful for laboratory management, but they do not fully describe the contribution of laboratory services to patient care. A more complete assessment should consider the total testing process, from test requesting and specimen collection to result reporting and clinical interpretation. Pre-analytical problems, analytical failures, delays in the availability of results, and errors in post-analytical communication may affect clinical decision-making and the use of healthcare resources. However, laboratory performance indicators should be interpreted with caution, since changes in individual indicators do not necessarily translate into measurable changes in clinical outcomes. Their interpretation requires clearly defined measures, appropriate targets, trend analysis, and consideration of the clinical and organizational context. Performance dashboards should be used as part of a quality-improvement process, with relevant findings investigated and corrective actions assessed over time. This approach is consistent with value-based laboratory medicine, which considers laboratory performance in relation to clinical care and patient safety. Integration of laboratory data with clinical information, outcome data, and emerging artificial intelligence tools may further improve this assessment, provided that their clinical validity, data quality, interoperability, and safety are adequately addressed.

title: Berta, an Open-Source, Modular AI Scribe for Clinical Documentation: Implementation Report.
desc: [JMIR medical informatics] Clinical documentation is a major contributor to physician workload and burnout, particularly in high-acuity settings such as emergency departments. Ambient AI scribes have emerged as a response, but commercial products cost US $99 to more than US $600 per physician per month, operate as opaque systems, and often process data on vendor-controlled infrastructure. These characteristics limit organizational control over data sovereignty, quality improvement, and clinical workflows and create barriers to adoption in resource-constrained settings. We aimed to develop an open-source, modular AI scribe platform that could be deployed entirely within institutional infrastructure, and to evaluate its real-world use across a provincial health system. We developed Berta, an open-source, modular platform that pairs a Next.js front end and a FastAPI back end with configurable automatic speech recognition and large language model components. A closed-source implementation developed in parallel with Berta was deployed at Alberta Health Services (AHS), Canada's largest provincially integrated health system at the time of implementation, and operated within AHS's existing Snowflake AI Data Cloud infrastructure. All clinical audio and text remained within the secure AHS environment. Use and session metadata were automatically recorded during routine clinical use by emergency physicians across AHS between November 2024 and July 2025, and physicians were emailed an optional survey. Operating costs were estimated from Snowflake service consumption over the same period. During the 9-month study period, 197 emergency physicians registered at 105 urban and rural facilities used the system, generating 21,548 clinical sessions and more than 2700 hours of audio. Monthly session volume grew from 675 sessions in November 2024 to 5463 in July 2025. Mean recorded session length was 7.6 minutes, and 42% (82/197) of users customized at least 1 documentation template. Operating costs averaged less than US $30 per physician per month, representing a 70% to 95% reduction in cost compared with commercial subscription prices; this comparison excludes personnel costs for development and maintenance. Survey respondents (69-73 per item) rated user-friendliness as good (median 5, IQR 4-6), reported a median time saving of 16 to 30 (IQR 0-15 to 46-60) minutes per shift, and rated documentation quality the lowest. After the pilot, access was opened to other departments, and by September 30, 2026, ap

title: Benchmarking Clinical Safety and Diagnostic Accuracy of Large Language Models in Otorhinolaryngology Emergencies: A Cross-Lingual Comparison of ChatGPT 5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro.
desc: [Ear, nose, & throat journal] BackgroundWhile the clinical potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) is increasingly recognised, their safety in morphologically rich languages remains debated. This exploratory study comparatively examines the ability of two recent artificial intelligence models, ChatGPT 5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro, to evaluate simulated otorhinolaryngology (ENT) cases across urgent, priority, and elective triage categories in Turkish and English.MethodsThe study was designed around 30 standardised clinical scenarios covering frequent ENT pathologies. Gold standard diagnosis and disease management decisions were determined by expert consensus. Model performance was evaluated in terms of three-category triage accuracy, clinical safety scores, and emergency-detection performance, using expert consensus decisions as the reference standard. Cohen's Kappa, Wilcoxon Signed Ranks, and McNemar tests were applied to measure inter-model and inter-language agreement.ResultsAll 120 model-generated primary diagnoses were confirmed as correct by the two ENT specialists. Correct triage classifications were obtained in 55/60 (91.7%) responses for ChatGPT 5.2 and 58/60 (96.7%) responses for Gemini 3 Pro. Agreement with expert-defined triage decisions was almost perfect (κ = 0.813-0.938). No statistically significant differences in the evaluated paired comparisons of triage accuracy or clinical safety scores were detected (all p > 0.05). Gemini 3 Pro correctly identified all 18 emergency scenarios in both language conditions.ConclusionsBoth models demonstrated high observed diagnostic and triage accuracy in a limited set of simulated ENT scenarios spanning different acuity levels. Although no statistically significant differences were detected in the evaluated comparisons, these findings do not establish equivalence between models or languages. These encouraging findings, particularly the high performance observed in Turkish, support further investigation of large language models as potential adjunctive clinical decision-support tools, while larger and more diverse clinical studies remain necessary before routine clinical implementation.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Precision Phytomedicine: A Critical Review and the Patient-Product-Mechanism-Response (PPMR) Framework.
desc: [Phytotherapy research : PTR] Plant-derived preparations remain widely used, yet their clinical application is constrained by multicomponent composition, batch-to-batch chemical variability, and complex pharmacokinetics, poorly characterized interactions, and marked interindividual variability in response. Artificial intelligence (AI) and computational pharmacology offer analytical tools suited to the high-dimensional data generated by phytomedicine, but enthusiasm has outpaced the supporting evidence. This critical narrative review evaluates AI applications across the phytomedicine pipeline, grading them by the strength and directness of evidence from computational prediction through in vitro, animal, observational, and randomized clinical studies. We organize the field around a Patient-Product-Mechanism-Response (PPMR) framework, arguing that meaningful personalization requires joint characterization of both the patient and the chemically variable botanical product. Current applications are most mature for botanical authentication, spectral annotation, quality assurance, and mechanism-informed hypothesis generation, whereas validated tools for patient stratification, individualized product and dose selection, and improved clinical outcomes remain limited. Rather than claiming efficacy gains, we present AI as a means to advance standardized, mechanism-informed, and testable phytomedicine, contingent on higher-quality data, prospective external validation, and regulatory alignment. The central finding is that none of the studies examined demonstrated a complete AI-guided personalized-phytomedicine pathway from joint patient-and-product characterization through a prospectively validated individualized response; precision phytomedicine should therefore be described as an emerging and hypothesis-generating research programme rather than an established clinical capability.

title: Near-Infrared Neuromodulation: Principles, Nanotechnology-Enabled Platforms, and Emerging Biomedical Frontiers.
desc: [ACS nano] Optogenetics enables highly specific regulation of neuronal activity with exceptional spatiotemporal precision, providing powerful tools for neural circuit interrogation and the treatment of neurological disorders. However, the limited tissue penetration of visible light restricts its application to deep neural tissues. Near-infrared (NIR) neuromodulation has emerged as a promising alternative by leveraging the superior tissue penetration and minimal invasiveness of NIR light. Recent advances in NIR-responsive nanomaterials, optical engineering, and neurotechnology have rapidly transformed the field from nonspecific photobiomodulation to cell-specific nanotransducer-mediated neuromodulation and integrated neuromodulation systems. In this review, we summarize the optical principles governing NIR propagation in biological tissues and the mechanisms underlying NIR-mediated neural stimulation. We then discuss recent advances in representative NIR nanotransducers, including photothermal, optoelectric, photoacoustic, and NIR-to-visible upconversion platforms together with integrated neuromodulation systems that combine NIR stimulation with multimodal neural recording and closed-loop feedback. We further highlight emerging applications in the central nervous system, optic nerve, and peripheral nerve disorders. Finally, we discuss the key challenges toward clinical translation, including improving tissue penetration, cell specificity, biosafety, and translation, developing intelligent multidisciplinary neuromodulation platforms, and integrating artificial intelligence with closed-loop neural interfaces to achieve adaptive, precise, and personalized neuromodulation.

title: Large language model-assisted modern programming pedagogy model: a perspective on teaching programming in the era of LLMs.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Large language models (LLMs) are a double-edged technology. They can serve as learning assistants in programming while simultaneously raising pedagogical and ethical concerns. Programming education researchers have responded by providing guidelines and recommendations on teaching, assessment, and the ethical use of LLMs. Although these developments are welcome, the literature still lacks theory-based frameworks that provide a philosophical grounding for programming pedagogy. This perspective paper addresses this gap by proposing the LLM-Assisted Modern Programming Pedagogy (LAMPP) model. The model aims to provide a theory-informed framework for systematically guiding the integration of LLMs into programming pedagogy. It proposes four design principles encompassing the core components of pedagogy (i.e., teaching, lesson design, engagement, and assessment). Ethics is included as an additional dimension because ethical concerns cut across all aspects of pedagogy. The LAMPP model proposes different mechanisms that may mitigate potential learning losses associated with inappropriate or excessive reliance on LLMs. Future studies should test the effectiveness of these mechanisms. The model may provide a basis for educators, researchers, and policymakers when considering policies, curriculum structures, course outcomes, assessment practices, and ethical guidelines related to programming pedagogy. In summary, it is not about LLM tools themselves but about the pedagogical orchestration of these technologies in programming education.

title: Multimodal Large Language Model Discrimination of Poster-to-Manuscript Conversion at the 2022-2023 Society of Surgical Oncology Annual Meetings.
desc: [Annals of surgical oncology] Whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) can identify publishable scientific work is untested. This study evaluated whether GPT-4.1 mini could distinguish Society of Surgical Oncology (SSO) posters that reached full-text publication using poster content alone and examined characteristics associated with conversion. This study retrospectively analyzed 597 posters from the 2022-2023 SSO Annual Meetings. Each poster was scored by GPT-4.1 on five research-quality domains during 30 runs at temperature zero. Discrimination was assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Multivariable logistic regression tested whether the score added information beyond poster and investigator characteristics. Of 597 posters, 295 (49.4%) reached full-text publication. The composite score showed modest discrimination (AUC, 0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.57-0.66), with no evidence that performance differed across categories (interaction P = 0.90). Each 5-point increase in score was associated with higher adjusted odds of publication (odds ratio [OR], 1.45; 95% CI, 1.21-1.75), and adding the score to poster characteristics improved discrimination (ΔAUC, 0.05; 95% CI, 0.01-0.08). Design rigor, data quality, conclusion validity, and publication potential scores were associated with publication, but novelty was not. Multicenter status, first-author training status, and author sex were not significantly associated with publication. Lower adjusted odds for Hispanic first authors did not persist after multiplicity correction (OR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.15-0.81). The GPT-4.1 mini scores modestly distinguished posters that reached publication and added information beyond poster characteristics. Multimodal large language models merit further study as instruments for examining and strengthening scholarly work rather than as arbiters of publishability.

title: Mammalian sperm selection in vivo and in vitro: an evolutionary perspective on advanced ICSI techniques.
desc: [Reproduction (Cambridge, England)] Fertilisation in mammals is preceded by a multilayered selection process shaped by more than 600 million years of evolution. The female reproductive tract acts as a sequential filter-through vaginal pH, cervical mucus, the uterotubal junction, the isthmic sperm reservoir, the cumulus matrix and the zona pellucida-such that only a few hundred capacitated, structurally and molecularly competent spermatozoa reach the ampulla. Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), introduced in 1992, bypasses these filters. Advanced techniques-including IMSI, physiological ICSI (PICSI), magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS), microfluidic sorting and deep-learning image classification-aim to restore part of this discriminatory capacity in the laboratory. Systematic reviews and current professional guidance indicate that none has produced a robust improvement in cumulative live birth in unselected assisted-reproduction populations, although ESHRE considers microfluidic selection an option. This review maps each technique to the in vivo filter it purports to mimic, evaluates the clinical evidence, considers long-term follow-up of ICSI-conceived offspring and imprinting-disorder surveillance, and asks whether targeted, mechanism-based selection in defined subgroups could succeed where unselected use has not. Evidence from non-human mammals-colloid and microfluidic selection in horses and cattle, sex-sorted semen, species differences in ICSI efficiency and mouse ICSI with DNA-damaged spermatozoa-is used to test the framework where human data are observational only. The evolutionary perspective is used as a design framework: for each technique, it identifies the mechanism to be recapitulated and the maternal, pregnancy and offspring outcomes by which benefit and safety should be judged.

title: Artificial intelligence for intimate apparel fit and comfort from technical evidence to business governance.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Artificial intelligence (AI) for intimate apparel supports body measurement, size and product recommendation, garment simulation, and virtual try-on, but these tasks provide different evidence about fit and comfort. This critical narrative review examines direct bra research alongside adjacent apparel technologies and identifies the validation needed for business use. Recent direct studies include machine-learning models of breast morphology, bra recommendation prototypes, finite-element contact models, dynamic scanning, pressure measurements, and longitudinal wearer research. They establish meaningful component-level progress, while leaving uncertainty about transfer across products and populations and about the causal effects of AI-assisted decisions on customer and financial outcomes. Two-dimensional image quality, three-dimensional geometric agreement, physical support, perceived comfort, and business impact are therefore evaluated separately. An operational transfer test distinguishes methodological relevance from evidence of successful domain transfer. Building on the evidence gaps, the review proposes task-specific evaluation priorities, safeguards for intimate body data, and a staged research agenda with explicit resource and decision requirements. These proposals are analytical contributions, not empirically validated maturity models or deployment guarantees. The central implication is that businesses should match each proposed claim to its measured outcome and scale investment only after the relevant technical, wearer, and operational evidence is established.

title: From silos to systems: a retrospective application of the measurement for change (M4C) framework to Grenada's intersectoral early childhood development strategy.
desc: [Frontiers in public health] Public health systems are often organized around single-sector mandates even when population needs span multiple sectors. Measurement for Change (M4C) was developed within early childhood development (ECD) to position monitoring, evaluation, and learning as a continuous process of adaptation, organized around five aspirations: Dynamic, Inclusive, Informative, Interactive, and People-centered. Whether these aspirations usefully describe national, intersectoral policy development remains largely untested. We conducted a retrospective qualitative case study examining the development of Grenada's Intersectoral Early Childhood Development (IECD) Strategy 2026-2030. Over 24 months, the process combined a desk review, 55 key-informant interviews, 34 focus groups, and eight parish-level consultations engaging over 400 participants, together with thematic and SWOT analysis, Theory of Change development, governance design, and costed implementation planning. Qualitative coding combined independent human coding with large-language-model-assisted comparison. M4C was not used prospectively to structure this process; rather, the completed process was examined afterward through the five M4C aspirations to assess convergence, tension, and implications for national-level application. The process showed strong convergence with all five aspirations, particularly through iterative stakeholder engagement, cross-sector and geographic participation, and translation of evidence into a costed Theory of Change and governance architecture. However, national-level application also exposed limits not evident at program scale. Political favoritism and institutional turf-protection constrained interactivity even where formal governance structures existed. Dynamism depended on institutional capacity to sustain ongoing review and adaptation after external technical support ended. Inclusion required disaggregation fine enough to reveal sub-national inequity. Some politically sensitive priorities, once surfaced, proved harder to act on than to identify. M4C provides a useful analytic lens for national systems-building, but at this scale its aspirations depend on enabling conditions such as political neutrality, institutional continuity, data harmonization, and decision authority that program-level applications can more readily assume.
